props.children: This section showcases the comprehensive exploratory visualizations from Visualization.ipynb. These charts reveal the strong price skewness, spatial micro-clustering, exponential relationships with living space, and the massive valuation premium of waterfront and architectural grade.
1. Real Map: House Locations & Price Distribution (King County)
Geographic scatter map of 5,000 sampled transactions on OpenStreetMap. Bubble size encodes interior living square footage; color represents sale price ($175k to $1.96M quantile range).

title.text: Real Map: House Locations & Prices across King County (OpenStreetMap)

props.children: 2. Price Skewness & The Power of Log Transformation

Raw real estate prices exhibit extreme positive skewness (+4.02) with high-value luxury tails. Applying np.log1p(price) transforms the distribution into a near-normal Gaussian bell curve (+0.43 skewness), stabilizing variance and boosting ML regression performance.

title.text: Price Distribution: Raw Skewness vs Log-Normalized Gaussian Curve

props.children: 3. Living Area vs Raw Price vs Log Price (Linearized Fit)

Comparing living square footage against raw price (left) reveals exponential fan-out heteroscedasticity. In contrast, plotting against log price (right) yields a tightly linearized relationship with consistent variance across all construction grades.

annotations.text: Living Area vs Log Price (Linearized Fit)

title.text: Living Area vs Price: Why Log Transformation Linearizes the Relationship

props.children: 4. Lot Size Analysis & Living-to-Lot Space Ratio

Left: Living Area vs Lot Area plotted on a logarithmic y-axis reveals the spread between compact urban parcels and vast suburban/rural acreage. Right: The engineered living_to_lot_ratio shows high-density urban properties commanding premium prices per land footprint.

annotations.text: Living Area vs Lot Area (Log Scale) vs Price

title.text: Lot Space & Density: Lot Area Analysis vs Living-to-Lot Ratio

props.children: Pearson correlation coefficients between top numerical housing features and sale price. Construction Grade (+0.67), Living Area (+0.70), and Sqft Living of 15 Neighbors (+0.59) stand out as the strongest single linear drivers.

props.children: Why We Selected XGBoost as the Champion Model

props.className: d-flex align-items-center gap-2 mb-3 pb-2 border-bottom

props.children: During our experimental evaluation in MachineLearning.ipynb, we trained and rigorously benchmarked four competing regression paradigms: Ordinary Linear Regression, Regularized Polynomial Ridge Regression (degree 2), Random Forest Regressor (100 estimators), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost Regressor). XGBoost decisively outperformed all other models across every key metric. Below are the core technical justifications:

Real estate prices are deeply non-linear. The value of an extra 500 square feet depends radically on location (Medina vs. Auburn) and construction grade. While linear regression requires explicit polynomial crosses that explode feature dimensionality, XGBoost's decision tree ensembles naturally identify multi-way feature interactions (e.g., Waterfront × Grade × Living Area) without manual combinatorial engineering.

On King County's 4,323 test homes, XGBoost achieved an R² score of 0.9098 (explaining ~91% of price variance) and reduced the Mean Absolute Error to $64,599. Compared to Ordinary Linear Regression ($113,987 MAE), XGBoost saved over $49,300 in error per house, and surpassed Random Forest by >$7,800 MAE and 2.0% in R².

Unlike standard Gradient Boosting Machines or deep neural nets, XGBoost formulates its objective function with native L1 (Lasso) and L2 (Ridge) penalties on tree leaf weights. Along with tree depth constraints (max_depth=6) and column subsampling (colsample_bytree=0.8), XGBoost effectively prevents overfitting even across King County's diverse micro-markets.

Random Forest builds independent trees and averages them (bagging). In contrast, XGBoost builds sequential trees where each new tree focuses specifically on the pseudo-residuals of previous trees. This iterative boosting mechanism excels at predicting rare luxury and edge-case properties that bagging and linear regressions consistently misprice.

Latitude and Longitude do not correlate linearly with price; prime housing borders irregular lakefronts and micro-neighborhoods. XGBoost's axis-aligned recursive splits partition latitude and longitude into high-value geographical bounding boxes, accounting for 16.0% of the model's total predictive power.

XGBoost's highly optimized C++ engine features cache-aware data structures and parallelized tree traversal. When users type feature inputs or click the map in this dashboard, the valuation is generated in less than 5 milliseconds, delivering a lightning-fast interactive web application experience.
The dataset contains 21,612 historical house sales in King County, WA (including Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Kirkland, and surrounding areas).
